params.title: Digital Logic
params.subtitle: From 1s and 0s to gates, flip-flops, memory and microprocessors: how the digital side of a radio works.

onScreen: From 1s and 0s to gates, flip-flops, memory and microprocessors
scenes.narration: Welcome to Digital Logic. A modern radio is full of small digital circuits. They tune it to the right channel, show numbers on its display, remember your settings, and run the whole set from a tiny computer called a microprocessor. All of it works with just 2 values, 1 and 0. We'll start from what a digital signal is, then build up to logic gates, the chips they're made in, circuits that remember or keep time, memory, microprocessors, converters and counters. No background is assumed. By the end, you'll be able to work out a gate diagram step by step and answer every exam question on digital logic.

params.title: Analog and digital signals
items: Analog: a voltage that can take any value, like a light on a dimmer
Digital: only 2 levels, high and low, like a light switch
The 2 levels stand for the 2 binary digits, 1 and 0
Bit: a single binary digit, one 1 or one 0

onScreen: Analog: any value, like a dimmer
Digital: only high and low, like a switch
High and low stand for 1 and 0
scenes.narration: What makes a signal digital? A signal is a voltage that carries information, and voltage is the electrical push in a circuit, measured in volts. An analog signal, such as a microphone's sound, can take any voltage and change smoothly, like a light on a dimmer. A digital signal has only 2 levels, high and low, like a light switch. Those 2 levels stand for 1 and 0, the only digits in binary, a way of counting we'll meet shortly. A single 1 or 0 is called a bit, short for binary digit. Since a circuit only has to tell high from low, a little noise, the random electrical disturbance on every wire, doesn't change the message.

params.title: Which level means 1? Positive and negative logic

scenes.narration: So a high level and a low level stand for 1 and 0. But which is which? That's a choice the designer makes, called the logic convention. In a positive-logic circuit, the high level represents logic 1 and the low level represents logic 0. That's the natural choice, and it's the one this lesson uses. In a negative-logic circuit, the convention is reversed: the high level represents logic 0, and the low level represents logic 1. On the exam, watch for choices like positive-transition level or negative-transition level. A transition is the moment a signal changes, not a level, so those are never the answer.

A single bit can only say 1 or 0. To carry a bigger number, digital circuits line up several bits in a row, and that row is a binary number. It works like the decimal numbers you use every day, just with fewer digits. Decimal has 10 digits, 0 to 9, so each place is worth 10 times the place to its right: thousands, hundreds, tens and ones. Binary has only 2 digits, 0 and 1, so each place is worth 2 times the place to its right. With 4 bits, the place values are 8, 4, 2 and 1, from left to right.

params.title: Writing the quantity 2 in binary
steps: Binary uses only the digits 0 and 1

scenes.narration: Time to write a number. Put a 1 in each place you need, and a 0 in the rest. The exam asks how to write the quantity 2. With place values 8, 4, 2 and 1, you need only the place worth 2. So it's 0 times 8, plus 0 times 4, plus 1 times 2, plus 0 times 1, which adds up to 2. Remember, binary uses only the digits 0 and 1, so every empty place gets a 0. The quantity 2 is written 0 0 1 0. The wrong choices, 0 0 0 2, 2 0 0 0 and 0 0 2 0, all contain the digit 2, which binary never uses.

params.title: Logic gates and truth tables
items: Logic gate: a circuit that makes a yes-or-no decision from its inputs
1 or more input bits in, 1 output bit out
Truth table: every input combination with its output
It describes a digital device's function; nothing to do with op-amps

onScreen: Input bits in, 1 output bit out
Truth table: every input combination and its output
scenes.narration: Bits can also make decisions. A logic gate is a circuit that makes a yes-or-no decision from its inputs. It takes 1 or more input bits and gives 1 output bit, following a fixed rule. To describe that rule, we use a truth table: a list of every combination of inputs, with the output each one gives. With 2 inputs, each 0 or 1, there are 2 times 2, or 4, combinations: 0 0, 0 1, 1 0 and 1 1. On the exam, a truth table is a list of input combinations and their corresponding outputs that characterizes, or describes, a digital device's function. The wrong choices tie it to op-amps, or operational amplifiers, which are analog, not digital.

params.title: The AND gate: all inputs must be 1

scenes.narration: The first gate is the AND gate. Picture a lamp wired through 2 switches, one after the other. The lamp lights only if the first switch and the second switch are both closed. An AND gate works the same way: it produces a logic 1 at its output only if all of its inputs are logic 1. Look down its truth table. Only the last row, with both inputs at 1, gives a 1. A 0 at any input forces the output to 0. The exam's wrong choices describe a 1 when only one input is 1, or when all the inputs are 0. Neither of those is an AND gate.

params.title: The OR gate: any 1 input gives a 1

scenes.narration: Next is the OR gate. This time, picture the 2 switches side by side, each one able to light the lamp on its own. Close either one, or both, and the lamp lights. An OR gate produces a logic 1 at its output if any input is logic 1. It gives a 0 only when every input is 0, which is the top row of its truth table. Compare that with the AND gate. AND needs all of its inputs to be 1, while OR is happy with any one. The other exam choices give a 0 when an input is 1, or a 1 only when every input is 0. Those describe inverted gates, which come next.

params.title: The NOT gate, or inverter
items: 1 input and 1 output: it flips the signal
Input 1 gives output 0; input 0 gives output 1
Symbol: a triangle with a small bubble at the output
On any gate symbol, the bubble means the output is inverted

onScreen: 1 in gives 0 out; 0 in gives 1 out
scenes.narration: AND and OR each combine 2 or more inputs. The simplest gate of all, the NOT gate, also called an inverter, has just 1 input and 1 output, and it flips the signal. A NOT gate produces a logic 0 at its output when the input is logic 1, and a logic 1 when the input is logic 0. A wrong choice on the exam gives a 1 out for a 1 in, which changes nothing at all. The NOT symbol is a triangle with a small circle, called a bubble, at the output. Remember that bubble. Wherever you see it on a gate symbol, it means the output is inverted. That's the key to the next 2 gates.

params.title: NAND: an AND gate followed by an inverter

scenes.narration: Put an inverter right after an AND gate, and you get a NAND gate, short for not-AND. Its symbol is the AND shape with a bubble on the output. Every AND output is simply flipped. AND gives a 1 only when all inputs are 1, so NAND gives a 0 only when all inputs are 1. Every other combination gives a 1. That's the exam's answer: a NAND gate produces a logic 0 at its output only when all inputs are logic 1. A handy way to remember it: any low input makes a NAND output high.

params.title: NOR: an OR gate followed by an inverter

scenes.narration: The same trick on an OR gate gives a NOR gate, short for not-OR: the OR shape with a bubble on the output. OR gives a 1 if any input is 1, so NOR gives a 0 if any input is 1. A NOR gate produces a logic 0 at its output if any or all inputs are logic 1. Its output is 1 only when every input is 0, the top row of the table. Be careful with the trap choice that says a NOR gives a 0 only if all inputs are 0. That's backwards: all 0s is the one case where a NOR gives a 1.

One more gate appears on the exam: the XOR, or exclusive OR. It works like an OR gate with one case left out. Its output is 1 when exactly one input is 1, which means the inputs are different. When the inputs are the same, both 0 or both 1, its output is 0. The left-out case, both inputs at 1, is what exclusive means: one or the other, but not both. So you can think of an XOR gate as a difference detector. Its symbol looks like an OR gate with an extra curved line on the input side.

params.title: Both inputs high: which gate gives a high?
rows: 0: the one case where it goes low

scenes.narration: Now that you've met all 6 gates, try a favorite exam question: which gate gives an active high out when both inputs are active high? Active high means a signal counts as on, or active, when it's high: a 1. So put a 1 on both inputs of each gate in the choices. AND gives a 1, because all its inputs are 1. NAND gives a 0, because that's the one case where it goes low. NOR gives a 0, because an input is high. And XOR gives a 0, because its inputs are equal. So the answer is the AND gate. An OR gate would give a high too, but it isn't among the choices.

params.title: Reading a gate diagram
items: H marks a high input; L marks a low input
Positive logic: H is 1 and L is 0
Start at the inputs and take 1 gate at a time
Write down each gate's output, then carry it to the next gate

onScreen: Positive logic: H is 1, L is 0
Start at the inputs, 1 gate at a time
Carry each output to the next gate
scenes.narration: Real circuits chain gates together, with one gate's output feeding the next. The exam has 3 such diagrams, Figures 3E12, 3E13 and 3E14, and asks for the levels at test points A, B and C. A test point is simply a spot in the circuit where you could touch a tester. The inputs are marked H for a high level and L for a low level. The questions say to assume positive logic, so H is 1 and L is 0. The method is always the same. Start at the inputs, take one gate at a time, work out its output from its rule, and carry that level along the wire to the next gate.

params.title: Figure 3E12: find test points A, B and C

callouts.label: Positive logic: H is high (1), L is low (0)
Top AND gets the inverted H, a low, so test point A is low
Bottom AND gets the inverted L (now high) with H, so test point B is high
OR gate: input B is high, so test point C is high
Answer: A is low, B is high and C is high

onScreen: Top AND gets inverted H: A is low
Bottom AND gets inverted L and H: B is high
A low, B high, C high
scenes.narration: Let's try it on Figure 3E12, with positive logic: H is 1, L is 0. Start at the top. H passes through an inverter and becomes a low, so the AND gate feeding point A has a low input. Any 0 input makes an AND output 0, so point A is low. Now the bottom. L passes through its inverter, becomes a high, and meets H at the AND gate. Both inputs are high, so test point B is high. Finally, the OR gate. Its inputs are A, low, and B, high. An OR gate needs only 1 high input, so test point C is high. The answer: A is low, B is high and C is high.

params.title: Figure 3E13: find test points A, B and C

callouts.label: Only NAND gates: any low input makes the output high
NAND making A sees L and H, so test point A is high
Top NAND sees L and point A, so test point B is high
Lower NAND sees point A and H, both high, so it outputs low
Output NAND gets that low, so test point C is high
Answer: all 3 test points are high

onScreen: Only NAND gates: any low input gives a high
NAND sees L and H: A is high
Top NAND sees L and A: B is high
Lower NAND sees A and H: low
scenes.narration: Next, Figure 3E13. It uses only NAND gates, again with positive logic. Remember: a NAND outputs 0 only when all its inputs are 1, so any low input makes its output high. The NAND gate making test point A sees L and H. It has a low input, so point A is high. The top NAND sees L and point A. Again there's a low input, so test point B is high. The lower NAND sees point A and H, both high, so its output is low. The output NAND gets B, which is high, and that low from the lower gate. With a low input, it makes test point C high. So all 3 test points are high.

params.title: Inside a gate: transistors on a chip
items: Current: the flow of electric charge, pushed by voltage
Transistor: a tiny electronic switch and amplifier
A small current controls a much larger current through it
IC, integrated circuit: many transistors on a single chip of silicon

onScreen: Transistor: a tiny switch and amplifier
A small current controls a larger one
scenes.narration: One figure is left, but its trap depends on how real chips behave. So what's inside a real gate? Transistors. To see what they do, you need one more idea: current, the flow of electric charge through a circuit, pushed along by voltage. Think of water in a pipe: voltage is the pressure, and current is the flow. A transistor is a tiny electronic switch and amplifier. A small current into one of its 3 terminals, or connections, controls a much larger current through it, the way a small tap handle controls a big flow of water. Thousands of transistors can be made together on one small chip of silicon, and that chip is called an integrated circuit, or IC.

params.title: TTL: transistor-transistor logic
items: TTL: transistor-transistor logic
Bipolar transistors do the gating and the output amplification
Gating: the logic decision; amplification: driving the output
Not resistor-transistor, diode-transistor or emitter-coupled logic

onScreen: Gating decides; amplification drives the output
Not resistor-, diode- or emitter-coupled logic
scenes.narration: Gates can be built from transistors in several ways, called logic families. A very common one is TTL, which stands for transistor-transistor logic. It gets that name because bipolar transistors, the classic type, do both jobs in the gate. They do the gating, which makes the logic decision from the inputs. And they do the output amplification, which drives the output strongly enough to feed the next gates. On the exam, resistor-transistor logic and diode-transistor logic are wrong. Those older families take their names from the parts at their inputs: resistors, or diodes, which are one-way valves for current. In TTL, transistors handle the inputs too. Emitter-coupled logic is a different family again.

params.title: TTL runs on a 5 volt supply
items: Power supply: the steady DC voltage that runs the chip
Common supply for TTL series integrated circuits: 5 volts
12 volts or 13.6 volts would destroy them

scenes.narration: Like every chip, a TTL chip needs a power supply: a steady DC, or direct current, voltage that runs its transistors. Direct means the current flows one way only. The common power supply voltage for TTL series integrated circuits is 5 volts. That number is worth remembering, because the rest of TTL is built around it. Watch for 12 volts and 13.6 volts on the exam. Those are the supply voltages of a car or a boat, which run many mobile radios, so they look familiar. But either one would push far too much current through the chip's tiny transistors and destroy it. And 1 volt is far too little to run it.

params.title: TTL input levels on a 5 volt supply

scenes.narration: On a 5 volt TTL chip, what voltage counts as high, and what counts as low? A valid logic low input is 0 to 0.8 volts. In between, from 0.8 to 2.0 volts, is an undefined zone: a voltage there is neither a valid low nor a valid high, and the chip may read it either way. A valid logic high input is 2.0 to 5.5 volts. That gap is deliberate. With low and high kept well apart, a little electrical noise can't turn one into the other. On the exam, ranges like 1.0 to 1.5 volts or 1.5 to 3.0 volts reach into the undefined zone, so they're wrong. So are negative voltages, and voltages far above the supply.

params.title: An open TTL input floats high
items: Open input: connected to nothing
To read low, a TTL input must have current flowing out of it
Open: no current flows out, so the input acts high
Open inputs are not ignored, and do not go random

scenes.narration: Those zones are for an input that's connected to something. What happens to a TTL input that's left open, connected to nothing? You might guess it reads low, or random. It doesn't. To pull a TTL input low, whatever drives it has to draw a small current out of the input. An open input has nowhere for that current to go. Because no current flows out of the unconnected input, the gate behaves as if a high were applied. So TTL inputs left open develop a high logic state. The wrong answers say open inputs are ignored, go low, or give random states. Remember instead: an open input floats high. You'll need that in the very next figure.

callouts.label: The open XOR input floats high in TTL
XOR sees H and a high: both inputs equal, so test point A is low
Inverter turns H into a low; lower NAND sees 2 lows, so B is high
Output NAND has point A low, so test point C is high
Answer: A is low, B is high and C is high

onScreen: XOR inputs equal: A is low
Lower NAND sees 2 lows: B is high
A low, B high, C high
scenes.narration: Here's that figure: 3E14, with positive logic devices. Its trap is an XOR input marked open. Remember, an open TTL input floats high. So the XOR gate sees H and a high. Both inputs are high and equal, so test point A is low. Down below, the inverter turns H into a low. The lower NAND gate sees L and that low, 2 lows, so test point B is high. Finally, the output NAND gets point A, which is low. A low input makes a NAND output high, so test point C is high. The answer: A is low, B is high and C is high.

params.title: Checking a TTL logic circuit
rows: High, low or pulsing: the best choice

onScreen: Logic probe: best, shows high, low or pulsing
VOM or DMM: only an average voltage
Continuity tester: nothing about logic states
scenes.narration: Working out levels on paper is one thing. On a real circuit board, how do you check them? The best instrument for checking a TTL logic circuit is a logic probe. It's a pen-shaped tester: touch its tip to a test point, and its lights show directly whether the point is high, low, or pulsing with activity. A VOM, or volt-ohm-milliammeter, and a DMM, or digital multimeter, are everyday meters that show only an average voltage. A line switching between high and low thousands of times a second averages out to an in-between number, which isn't a logic state at all. And a continuity tester only checks whether a path is connected, so it shows nothing about logic states.

params.title: Flip-flops: circuits that remember
items: Gates have no memory: the output follows the inputs right now
Flip-flop: a binary sequential logic element
2 stable states: set and reset, 1 and 0
Holds its state until an input pulse switches it

onScreen: 2 stable states: set and reset, 1 and 0
Holds its state until a pulse switches it
scenes.narration: None of the gates so far has any memory. A gate's output follows its inputs, and once they change, the old answer is gone. But a radio must remember things, like the channel you picked. For that, circuits use a flip-flop. Think of a light switch again: flip it up and it stays up, flip it down and it stays down. A flip-flop is a binary sequential logic element with 2 stable states, states it can rest in, called set and reset, or 1 and 0. Sequential means its output depends on what happened before, not just on the inputs now. It holds its state until an input pulse, a quick jump from low to high and back, switches it.

params.title: 1 flip-flop stores 1 bit
items: A single flip-flop stores 1 bit of information
Register: a row of flip-flops holding a group of bits
R-S flip-flop: S sets it to 1, R resets it to 0
An 8 bit storage register needs 8 R-S flip-flops, 1 per bit

onScreen: R-S: S sets to 1, R resets to 0
scenes.narration: A flip-flop holds 1 of 2 states, and 1 of 2 states is exactly 1 bit. So a single flip-flop circuit stores 1 bit of information. To store a bigger number, line up several flip-flops side by side. That row is called a register. A common kind is the R-S, or reset-set, flip-flop. A signal on its S input sets it to 1, and a signal on its R input resets it to 0. How many R-S flip-flops would you need to construct an 8 bit storage register? One per bit position, so 8. Answers of 2, 4 or 16 don't give 1 flip-flop per bit.

params.title: The clock keeps a circuit in step
labels: CLK, the clock: a steady train of pulses
Clocked R-S: R and S act only when the clock pulses
In step with the clock: synchronous

onScreen: CLK: a steady train of clock pulses
R and S act only on a clock pulse
In step with the clock: synchronous
scenes.narration: The R-S flip-flop on the exam is a clocked one, with a few more inputs, so let's meet them one at a time. First, CLK, short for clock: a steady train of pulses that keeps a digital circuit in step, like a drummer keeping time for a band. In a clocked R-S flip-flop, the R and S inputs don't act the moment they change. They wait, and take effect only when the clock pulses. Acting in step with the clock like that is called synchronous. So an R-S flip-flop can accept data into its R-S inputs with CLK initiated, which is exam language for a clock pulse arriving.

params.title: PRE and CLR: inputs that skip the clock
rows: Clocked R and S are ignored

onScreen: S and R: act on the clock, synchronous
PRE or CLR active: R and S ignored
scenes.narration: S and R, as you've just seen, wait for the clock. But a clocked R-S flip-flop also has 2 inputs that don't. The first is PRE, for preset. It forces the output to 1 immediately, without the clock, and that's called asynchronous, meaning not in step with the clock. The second is CLR, for clear, which forces the output to 0, also asynchronously. So the flip-flop can accept data into its PRE and CLR inputs without CLK. They also take priority, like an override button. While one of them is active, the clocked R and S inputs are ignored. In exam words, the flip-flop can refuse synchronous data while asynchronous data is being input at the same time.

params.title: What an R-S flip-flop cannot do
items: Toggle: flip to the opposite state on every clock pulse
R and S held constant: each pulse just sets it again, or resets it again
So an R-S flip-flop cannot operate in toggle mode
Toggling is a J-K or T flip-flop function

onScreen: Toggle: flip on every clock pulse
R-S held constant: same state every pulse
scenes.narration: Now the exam's twist. It lists things an R-S flip-flop can do and asks for the one it can't. That one is operating in toggle mode with its R-S inputs held constant and CLK initiated. To toggle means to flip to the opposite state on every clock pulse: 1, 0, 1, 0. Hold S high and R low, and each clock pulse just sets the flip-flop again, so it stays at 1. Hold R high instead, and each pulse just resets it again. Either way, nothing flips. Toggling is a job for a J-K flip-flop, or a T, for toggle, flip-flop. It can do the other 3 choices: the clock, preset and clear behavior you've just met.

params.title: A toggling flip-flop halves the frequency
labels: Input: a pulse train; 1 cycle is a pulse and the gap after it
A toggling flip-flop changes state once per input cycle
Output: a square wave at half the input frequency

onScreen: Input pulse train: 1 cycle = a pulse and its gap
Toggling flip-flop: changes state once per cycle
Output: square wave at half the frequency
scenes.narration: Toggling turns out to be very useful, because it divides frequency. A pulse train's frequency is how many cycles arrive each second, where 1 cycle is one pulse and the gap after it. Feed a pulse train into a toggling flip-flop, a J-K or a T, and its output changes state once for each input cycle: high after the first pulse, low after the second, high after the third. So it takes 2 input cycles to make 1 complete output cycle. The output is a square wave, spending equal time high and low, at half the input frequency. Each toggling flip-flop divides its input frequency by 2.

Next, cascade a second flip-flop, which means feeding the first one's output into it. Follow the chain from the left. The input pulses go into flip-flop 1, which toggles and divides their frequency by 2. Its square wave then drives flip-flop 2, which toggles once per cycle of that wave and divides by 2 again. Half of a half is a quarter, so the final output is the input frequency divided by 4. Every flip-flop you add to the chain halves the frequency once more.

params.title: How many flip-flops to divide by 4?
steps: n = number of flip-flops in cascade

onScreen: Division = 2 to the power of n
scenes.narration: That gives us a rule. Each flip-flop divides by 2, so n flip-flops in cascade divide the frequency by 2 multiplied by itself n times, which is 2 to the power of n. Here, n stands for the number of flip-flops. The exam asks how many flip-flops are required to divide a signal frequency by 4. We need 2 to the power of n to equal 4. Try 1 flip-flop: 2 to the power of 1 is 2, not enough. Try 2: 2 to the power of 2 is 2 times 2, which is 4. So 2 flip-flops are required, just like the chain you saw. The trap answer is 4, which is the division, not the number of flip-flops.

params.title: 3 kinds of multivibrator
rows: Switches back and forth, no trigger input
Flips when triggered, returns after a set time
Holds 1 or 0 until triggered: a flip-flop

scenes.narration: The flip-flop has another name, and it opens a new topic: multivibrators. A multivibrator is a switching circuit built from 2 transistors, wired so that when one turns on, it turns the other off. So the circuit is always in one of 2 states: one transistor on, or the other. Multivibrators come in 3 kinds, named for how many of those states are stable, meaning the circuit can rest there. An astable multivibrator has no stable state, so it never rests. A monostable has 1 stable state. And a bistable has 2 stable states, which makes it the flip-flop we just met. The prefixes tell you: a means none, mono means 1, and bi means 2.

params.title: The bistable multivibrator is a flip-flop
items: Bistable multivibrator: 2 stable states, holds a 1 or a 0
Its common name: a flip-flop
Not a clock: a clock is astable and never stops switching
Not an AND or OR gate: gates have no memory

onScreen: Not a clock: a clock is astable
Not AND or OR: gates have no memory
scenes.narration: Start with the bistable, since you already know it. A bistable multivibrator circuit has 2 stable states, and it holds a 1 or a 0 until it's triggered. That's exactly a flip-flop, and flip-flop is its common name. The exam asks this 2 ways, what a bistable multivibrator is and what it's commonly named, and the answer to both is a flip-flop. The wrong choices are a clock, an AND gate and an OR gate. A clock is an astable circuit, because it never stops switching. And AND and OR gates have no memory, so they can't hold a state. None of them is a bistable multivibrator.

blocks.label: Bistable multivibrator
blocks.note: Changes state once per input cycle

blocks.label: Astable multivibrator
blocks.note: Makes its own signal: not a divider

onScreen: Bistable multivibrator: changes state once per cycle
Astable: makes its own signal, not a divider
scenes.narration: The bistable answers one more exam question: how can the frequency of an AC, or alternating current, signal be divided electronically? Alternating current swings back and forth in repeating cycles. Feed it to a bistable multivibrator, and the bistable changes state once per input cycle, just like the toggling flip-flop. 2 input cycles make 1 output cycle, so the output has half the input frequency: the bistable divides by 2. The trap answers are the astable, or free-running, multivibrator and the OR gate. An astable generates its own signal instead of following the input, and an OR gate has no memory to count cycles with.

params.title: The astable multivibrator: free-running
items: Alternates between 2 unstable states
No trigger input: it switches back and forth on its own
Free-running: a clock is an astable circuit

onScreen: No trigger: switches on its own
scenes.narration: The astable multivibrator is the opposite of the bistable: it never rests. It's a circuit that alternates between 2 unstable states. Unstable means the circuit can't stay there. As soon as it lands in one state, a capacitor, a part that stores electric charge, starts charging. Once it's charged far enough, it pushes the circuit over into the other state, and the same thing happens again. It's like a car's turn signal, blinking on and off by itself. It needs no trigger input, so it's called free-running, and that's why a clock is an astable circuit. On the exam, 2 stable states, or a stable and an unstable state, are wrong. A stable state would let it settle and stop.

params.title: Astable output: a square wave
labels: Collector outputs of the common-emitter stage: square waves
Each transistor snaps between fully on and fully off
Not a sine wave, a sawtooth or half-wave pulses

onScreen: Transistors snap fully on and fully off
Not sine, sawtooth or half-wave pulses
scenes.narration: What does an astable multivibrator's output look like? Each of its 2 transistors is wired in the common-emitter way, the standard amplifier hookup, and the output is taken from the transistor's collector, one of its 3 terminals. The voltage outputs at the collectors are square waves. That's because each transistor snaps between fully on and fully off, with almost no time in between. So the voltage jumps straight from low to high, stays there, and jumps back. That flat-topped shape is a square wave. It's not a sine wave, which curves smoothly, not a sawtooth, which ramps up slowly, and not half-wave pulses, the rounded bumps left when half of a sine wave is cut off.

params.title: The monostable multivibrator: a one-shot
items: 1 stable state, where it rests
A trigger switches it momentarily to the opposite binary state
After a set time, it returns to its original state
An RC network, a resistor and a capacitor, sets the time

onScreen: Trigger: switches to the opposite state
After a set time, it returns
scenes.narration: The third kind is the monostable, or one-shot, multivibrator. It has 1 stable state, where it rests. A trigger pulse can switch it momentarily to the opposite binary state, and after a set time, it returns to its original state on its own. That time is fixed by an RC, or resistor-capacitor, network: a resistor, which limits current, and a capacitor. The capacitor charges slowly through the resistor, and once it's charged far enough, the circuit flips back. Think of a stairwell light on a timer: it comes on when pressed, then turns itself off.

params.title: Matching the exam's descriptions
rows: A clock: a continuous square wave
Switched momentarily, returns after a set time
Stores 1 bit as a 0 or a 1

onScreen: Returns after a set time: monostable
scenes.narration: The exam describes these circuits in words and asks you to name them, and the monostable question uses the other kinds as its traps. A circuit that alternates between 2 unstable states is astable, and so is a clock, with its continuous square wave. A circuit that can be switched momentarily and then returns after a set time is monostable. A circuit that stores 1 bit as a 0 or a 1 is bistable, a flip-flop. And a circuit that holds a constant output voltage isn't a multivibrator at all: it's a voltage regulator. The quick way to remember: an astable never rests, a monostable rests in 1 state, and a bistable rests in either of 2.

params.title: Memory: a grid of bit cells
items: Memory cell: holds 1 bit
Location: a group of cells read or written together
Address: the number that picks a location
Address pins choose the location; data pins carry its bits

scenes.narration: Flip-flops and registers hold a few bits. A radio needs to hold thousands: its program, its channels, its settings. That's the job of a memory chip, our next topic. Inside is a grid, or matrix, of memory cells, each holding 1 bit. The cells are grouped into locations, and each location has its own number, called its address, like the house numbers on a street. The chip has 2 sets of pins. The address pins carry the address, choosing which location to use. The data pins carry that location's bits in or out. Memory chips differ in whether you can write to them, and in how they hold their bits.

params.title: RAM: random-access memory
items: RAM: random-access memory
Its digital data can be written or read
Any memory word address can be accessed directly, in any order
Not ROM, PROM or EPROM: those are read-only memories

scenes.narration: The first kind, and the everyday working memory, is RAM, which stands for random-access memory. Like every chip here, it's a semiconductor IC. Silicon is a semiconductor, the material transistors are made from. RAM is the semiconductor memory IC whose digital data can be written or read, and whose memory word address can be accessed randomly. A memory word is the group of bits at one address. Random access means jumping straight to any address, in any order, like opening a book at any page instead of winding through a tape. The wrong choices are ROM, read-only memory, and its programmable versions, PROM and EPROM. All 3 are programmed ahead of time, then only read in normal use.

params.title: ROM: read-only memory
items: ROM: read-only memory
A fixed pattern of digital data stored in its memory matrix
Can be read, but not changed
Not RAM, a register or a latch: those hold changing data

onScreen: Not RAM, a register or a latch
scenes.narration: ROM, or read-only memory, is the opposite case. ROM is the semiconductor IC that has a fixed pattern of digital data stored in its memory matrix. The pattern is set when the chip is made or programmed, and in use it can be read, but not changed. That makes ROM the right place for information that must never get lost, such as the instructions that start a radio. On the exam, the wrong choices are RAM, a register and a latch. A register, as you've seen, is a row of flip-flops, and a latch is a close cousin of the flip-flop. Both hold data that changes, so neither is a fixed pattern.

params.title: DRAM must be refreshed
items: DRAM: dynamic random-access memory
Each bit is stored as a charge on a tiny capacitor
The charge leaks away, so it must be refreshed periodically
Refresh: read each bit and write it back

onScreen: Each bit: charge on a tiny capacitor
scenes.narration: One kind of RAM needs constant attention. DRAM, or dynamic random-access memory, stores each bit as a charge on a tiny capacitor. A charged capacitor is one state and an empty one is the other. The trouble is that the charge slowly leaks away, like water from a leaky bucket. So DRAM must be refreshed periodically to keep reliable data: each bit is read and written back before it fades. On the exam, ROM, PROM and PRAM are the wrong choices. Only DRAM must be refreshed, and the word dynamic, meaning always changing, is your clue.

params.title: Each address pin doubles the locations

scenes.narration: How many cells does a memory chip hold? You can work it out from the address and data pins we met earlier. Start with the address pins. Each one carries 1 bit of the address, a 1 or a 0. With 1 pin, you can pick 2 locations. With 2 pins, there are 4 patterns, 0 0, 0 1, 1 0 and 1 1, so 4 locations. Every extra pin doubles the count: 3 pins pick 8, and 4 pins pick 16. So the number of locations is 2 to the power of the number of address pins: 2 multiplied by itself once for each pin.

params.title: How many memory cells?
steps: 4 data pins: 4 bits in each location

onScreen: cells = 2 to the power of the address pins × data pins
scenes.narration: Then add the data pins, and you have the formula: cells equal 2 to the power of the address pins, times the data pins. The exam's chip has 4 address pins, so it has 2 to the power of 4 locations: 2 times 2 times 2 times 2, which is 16. It also has 4 data bus input-output pins. Each data pin carries 1 bit in or out, so each location holds 4 bits. Now multiply: cells equal 16 locations times 4 bits each. That's 64 memory cells. Watch the traps: 16 is only the locations, and 8 just adds the pins together.

params.title: A microprocessor follows a program
items: Microprocessor: a chip that carries out instructions one after another
Program: a microprocessor's sequence of commands and instructions
I/O, input-output: ports and circuits to external devices

onScreen: Program: the sequence of commands and instructions
scenes.narration: Memory holds bits, and something has to use them. That's the microprocessor: a chip that reads instructions from memory and carries them out, one after another. Add 2 numbers, compare them, send a result to the display, then on to the next. The name for a microprocessor's sequence of commands and instructions is a program. Sequence, data string and data execution sound plausible on the exam, but the name is program. To reach the keypad, the display and the rest of the radio, the processor uses its I-O, usually written I slash O. Within a microprocessor system, I-O means input-output: the ports and circuits that move data between the microprocessor and external devices.

params.title: The clock and the ALU
items: Clock: the pulse generator of a microprocessor circuit
Its pulses step the processor through each instruction
Not the pulse generator: RAM and ROM are memory; a PLL controls frequency
ALU: arithmetical logic unit, does the arithmetic and logic

onScreen: RAM and ROM: memory; PLL: frequency control
scenes.narration: A microprocessor needs 2 more parts to do its work. The first is the clock, the pulse generator of a microprocessor circuit. It's a free-running circuit, like the astable multivibrator, and its pulses step the processor through each instruction, the way a drummer sets the beat. On the exam, the wrong choices for the pulse generator are RAM and ROM, which are memory, and a PLL, or phase-locked loop, which is a frequency-control loop that holds a radio's frequency steady. The second part is inside the processor: the ALU. In a microprocessor, ALU means arithmetical logic unit, the part that performs the arithmetic and logic operations, built from gates like the ones you've learned.

params.title: The watchdog timer
items: Watchdog timer: verifies the microprocessor is executing the program
The running program keeps resetting it
If the program stops resetting it, it times out and resets the processor
Not for frequency, power output or radar

onScreen: Watchdog: verifies the program is executing
Program stuck: it resets the processor
scenes.narration: As long as the clock keeps ticking, the processor works through its program. But sometimes a program gets stuck, perhaps after a burst of electrical noise, and a radio that freezes is useless. So a microprocessor-controlled two-way radio has a watchdog timer. The watchdog verifies that the microprocessor is executing the program. Think of a kitchen timer that the program must keep winding back before it rings. While the program runs normally, it keeps resetting the watchdog in time. If the program stops resetting it, the watchdog times out and resets the processor, which starts the program again. The wrong choices, keeping the transmission on frequency, limiting the power output, or connecting to the radar, are other circuits' jobs.

onScreen: Data bus line links processor, memory and I/O
scenes.narration: Now let's put the whole system on one page. The clock, the pulse generator, drives the microprocessor, with its ALU inside, and the watchdog timer keeps an eye on it. Below the processor sit RAM, then the data bus line, then ROM. The data bus line is the circuit that interconnects the microprocessor with the memory and the input-output system. A bus is a set of shared wires, like a bus route that serves every stop. Bits travel along it between the processor, RAM, ROM and the I-O, which reaches the external devices. The other exam choices, a control logic bus, a PLL line and a directional coupler, are not the answer.

params.title: The MCU: a computer on one chip
items: MCU: microcontroller unit
Contains the processor with RAM, ROM and I/O on one chip
Not part of the MCU: the voltage regulator
The voltage regulator is a separate external component

onScreen: Processor, RAM, ROM and I/O on one chip
Not part of it: the voltage regulator
scenes.narration: Imagine that whole page shrunk onto a single chip. That's a microcontroller, used in many radios instead of a separate microprocessor and memory chips. An MCU, or microcontroller unit, puts the processor, the RAM, the ROM and the I-O together on one chip: a complete small computer. So which of these is not part of an MCU processor: RAM, ROM, I-O or a voltage regulator? The voltage regulator. A voltage regulator is the circuit that holds the supply voltage steady, and it's a separate external component that feeds power to the chip.

Whether it's a microprocessor or an MCU, it only works with bits, but the world outside is analog: sound, signal strength, tuning voltages. Converters bridge the gap. An ADC, or analog-to-digital converter, is the integrated circuit device that converts an analog signal to a digital signal. It measures the voltage again and again and turns each measurement into a binary number. A DAC, or digital-to-analog converter, is the integrated circuit device that converts digital signals to analog signals, the reverse of an ADC. So in a microprocessor circuit, DAC means digital to analog converter. It turns binary values into a proportional voltage or current: a bigger number gives a bigger voltage.

params.title: A prescaler ahead of a frequency counter

blocks.label: HF signal
blocks.note: High frequency: too fast for the counter

onScreen: HF signal: too fast for the counter
Prescaler divides: it does not multiply
scenes.narration: The last topic, counters, takes us back to dividing flip-flops. Dividing frequency has a practical use: measuring it. A frequency counter counts the cycles that arrive in a set time and shows the result. But a simple counter can only count so fast, and an HF, or high frequency, signal can be too fast. The fix is a prescaler, a fast divider ahead of the counter. The purpose of a prescaler circuit is to divide an HF signal so that a low-frequency counter can display the operating frequency. It divides by a known factor, such as 10 or 100, and the reading is scaled back up by the same factor. The trap answer says it multiplies, but it divides.

blocks.label: 1 output pulse
blocks.note: Display decoding is a separate job

scenes.narration: A common divider inside a counter is the decade counter. Decade means 10. A decade counter digital IC counts input pulses from 0 up to 9, and on the 10th pulse it starts over and sends 1 pulse out. So its function is to produce 1 output pulse for every 10 input pulses: a divide-by-10 function. Chain decade counters, and each one counts one decimal digit: ones, tens, hundreds. As for the traps, 10 output pulses for every input pulse is backwards. Adding 2 decimal numbers is an adder's job. And decoding a decimal number for a seven-segment display, the number display made of 7 bars, is done by a separate decoder.

params.title: BCD: binary coded decimal
items: BCD: binary coded decimal
Each decimal digit, 0 through 9, gets its own 4-bit binary group
So 25 becomes 0010 0101

onScreen: Each decimal digit 0 through 9: its own 4-bit group
scenes.narration: Counters and displays like to handle numbers one decimal digit at a time, and that's where BCD comes in. BCD means binary coded decimal. Instead of turning a whole number into one long binary number, each decimal digit, 0 through 9, gets its own 4-bit binary group. Take the number 25. The 2 is written 0 0 1 0, using the place values 8, 4, 2 and 1, just as we did earlier. The 5 is 4 plus 1, so it's 0 1 0 1. Put the groups side by side, and in BCD, 25 becomes 0 0 1 0, 0 1 0 1. The wrong choices, like bit count decimal, just shuffle similar words.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: TTL: 5 volt supply; low 0 to 0.8 volts, high 2.0 to 5.5 volts; an open input floats high
AND needs all 1s, OR needs any 1, a bubble inverts: NOT, NAND, NOR
Flip-flop = bistable: 2 stable states, 1 bit; each one divides by 2
Memory cells = 2<sup>address pins</sup> × data pins; DRAM must be refreshed
Clock = pulse generator, data bus links all; ADC analog to digital, DAC back

onScreen: TTL: 5 volts, low 0 to 0.8, high 2.0 to 5.5, open floats high
AND, OR, and the inverting bubble
Flip-flop: 2 stable states, 1 bit, divides by 2
Cells = 2 to the power of address pins × data pins
Clock, data bus, ADC and DAC
scenes.narration: Let's pull it together. In positive logic, high is 1. TTL chips run on 5 volts: 0 to 0.8 volts is a valid low, 2.0 to 5.5 volts a valid high, and an open input floats high. AND needs all 1s, OR needs any 1, and a bubble inverts, giving NOT, NAND and NOR. Work every diagram one gate at a time. A flip-flop, or bistable multivibrator, has 2 stable states, stores 1 bit, and divides by 2. Memory cells equal 2 to the power of the address pins, times the data pins, and DRAM must be refreshed. Last, the clock is the pulse generator, the data bus links everything, and an ADC goes analog to digital, a DAC back.
